Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Essential File and Directory Management

Learn the commands and safety habits that let you create, reorganize, back up, and remove files and directories reliably on Linux.

Why this matters: these operations are the building blocks of installing software, configuring services, and maintaining system state. Mistakes can be simple or catastrophic, so clear procedures and checks matter.

Example workflow: create a project layout with mkdir -p, populate with touch, copy with cp -r, and use rm -ri when removing directories.

In this lesson
Commands to build and maintain directory structures, plus safe deletion practices and permission basics.
Explore Key Topics
Create
touch and mkdir -p let you set up files and nested directories in one step.
Move & Copy
cp -r and mv handle directories and files; mv renames or relocates without duplicating data.
Delete Safely
Use rmdir for empty dirs, rm -ri for interactive removal, and avoid rm -rf unless you are certain.
Visual Overview
Project setup
mkdir -p project/src && touch project/README.md
Backup
cp -r logs /tmp/backup_logs — copies entire directory trees.
Safe remove
rm -ri conf prompts before each deletion; rm -rf is immediate and dangerous.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Practice Tasks
Task cards

screens.title: Creating files and directories
screens.narratorSegment: Creating files and directories is one of the most frequent tasks you'll perform. The touch command creates an empty file when it doesn't exist and updates timestamps when it does; this is useful for quickly making placeholder files like README. md or logs/app. log. For directories, mkdir creates a single directory; adding the -p option lets you create a full nested path in one command. For example, mkdir -p projects/my_app/config builds every required parent automatically. This is faster and less error-prone than running multiple mkdir commands. A common misconception is that touch is only for empty files; in reality it also updates access and modification times which can be useful in build systems. A concrete example: mkdir -p src/main/java conf logs followed by touch src/main/java/App. java conf/config. properties logs/app. log creates a reproducible starter layout. Verification with ls -R shows the created tree. Tip: when scripting, mkdir -p prevents errors if the directory already exists. Takeaway: use touch for files and mkdir -p for nested directories to set up consistent structures quickly and predictably. Creating files and directories means use touch to create or update files and mkdir -p to create nested directories in a single, idempotent command.. In practical terms, using touch and mkdir -p to build and initialize project structures. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Create reliably
keyIdea.text: Use touch to create or update files and mkdir -p to create nested directories in a single, idempotent command.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Create
Definition & behavior

touch creates empty files or updates timestamps. mkdir -p creates nested directories, making the command idempotent across repeated runs.

Concrete example
mkdir -p my_project/src/main/java conf logs
cd my_project
touch src/main/java/App.java conf/config.properties logs/app.log README.md
ls -R
Key Takeaway

mkdir -p and touch let you reproducibly create project scaffolding. Always verify with ls -R.

Common mistake

Running mkdir without -p when parents don't exist will fail. Running touch with a wrong path will create files in the wrong directory if you are not in the intended working directory.

Practice scenario
You need a reproducible Java project skeleton. Use mkdir -p to create all directories, touch to create placeholders, then run ls -R to confirm hierarchy before adding code or version control.
Pro tip
When scripting, include mkdir -p at the start of scripts to ensure directories exist and avoid race conditions that cause scripts to fail on second runs.

screens.title: Copying files and directories
screens.narratorSegment: Copying is often used for backups, testing, or preparing alternate configurations. The cp command copies files with a simple source and destination syntax. For directories you must add -r to copy recursively, for example cp -r my_app_dir /srv/backup/ will duplicate the directory and its contents into the backup location. A common error is forgetting the -r option and receiving an error that the source is a directory. Another pitfall is confusing cp with mv: cp leaves the original intact while mv relocates it. A concrete example from the hands-on activity: cp conf/config. properties conf/config. bak creates a backup copy in place, while cp -r logs /tmp/backup_logs copies the whole logs tree. Verify copies via ls or by checking file sizes and counts. If you need to preserve permissions and timestamps, additional options exist, but at this stage remember the core difference: cp duplicates, mv moves. Misconception check: cp does not change ownership of the original file; it creates a new file owned by the user who ran the command unless special options are used. Takeaway: use cp -r for directories and always verify the destination.

keyIdea.title: Copy vs move
keyIdea.text: cp duplicates data (use -r for directories); mv relocates or renames without duplication. Always verify copied content with ls or size checks.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Copy
Command walkthrough
# Copy a single file
cp conf/config.properties conf/config.bak
# Copy a directory tree recursively
cp -r logs /tmp/backup_logs/
# Verify
ls conf
ls -R /tmp/backup_logs
Remember: cp leaves the original in place. If the destination exists and is a directory, cp will place the copy inside that directory.
Key Takeaway

Use cp -r for directories; forgetfulness about -r is a frequent source of errors.

Common mistake

Trying to copy directories without -r triggers an error. Always check whether your source is a file or directory before copying.

Scenario
You want to back up logs before rotation. Run cp -r logs /tmp/backup_logs and then compare ls -R output to ensure all subdirectories were copied. If size or counts differ, inspect for excluded files or permission issues.
Verification
Use ls -R and file counts to confirm the copy. If ownership differs unexpectedly, remember the copy will be owned by the user who performed the cp.

screens.title: Moving and renaming with mv
screens.narratorSegment: Moving and renaming are both handled by the mv command. The simplest form is mv source destination. If the destination is a new name in the same directory, mv performs a rename. If the destination is a directory path, mv relocates the source into that directory. Unlike cp, mv does not create a separate copy; it changes the filesystem location or name reference of the original. This behavior makes mv efficient for reorganizing files but also means that a mistaken mv can make the original path disappear. For example, mv old_name. txt new_name. txt renames a file, and mv config. yaml /etc/my_app/ moves it to the configuration directory. A common misconception is thinking mv requires -r for directories; it does not — moving a directory will move all contents implicitly. In scripts, adding checks such as testing destination existence or using mv -n to prevent overwriting can protect data. Always verify results with ls -R or by opening the moved files in their new location. Takeaway: mv moves or renames without duplication; use it when you want to reorganize rather than copy.

keyIdea.title: Move = relocate
keyIdea.text: mv renames or moves objects without copying their contents. It does not need -r for directories and can overwrite existing files unless protected.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Move
Step-by-step
Rename a file
mv old_name.txt new_name.txt
Move to another directory
mv config.yaml /etc/my_app/
Pro tip
Use mv -n to avoid overwriting existing files unintentionally when supported by your environment, and always confirm the destination path exists.
Scenario & verification
You reorganized source into a new language folder. Run mv src/main/java src/main/kotlin then rename App.java to Main.kt during the move. Verify with ls -R src to ensure files arrived as expected.
Key Takeaway

mv changes the location or name without duplicating data; use it for reorganizing but double-check paths to avoid unintended loss of visibility.

Common mistake

Assuming mv creates a copy. If you wanted a copy, use cp; mv will remove the original link at the old path.

screens.title: Removing files and directories safely
screens.narratorSegment: Deletion is the most dangerous daily operation if used without caution. Use rmdir only for empty directories; it fails if the directory contains files. For files, rm removes single files. To remove directories and their contents, rm -r recursively deletes everything inside. The -i flag makes rm interactive and prompts before each deletion, which can be a lifesaver when working in unfamiliar directories. The rm -rf combination is both recursive and forceful and will delete without prompts even for write-protected files — this is why rm -rf used in the wrong path can be catastrophic. A concrete example from the hands-on activity: rm -ri conf prompts you for each file before deleting, providing a safety net. Contrast that with rm -rf /tmp/backup_logs which deletes without confirmation. Misconception: some users expect the shell to prevent dangerous rm commands; it will not. Always double-check pwd and consider an alias or a habit of running ls before rm. Takeaway: prefer interactive removal during learning and retain backups to recover from mistakes. Removing files and directories safely means rmdir removes only empty directories; rm -r deletes recursively; rm -rf is immediate and dangerous. use rm -ri to prompt for safety.. In practical terms, rmdir, rm, rm -r, rm -i and the danger of rm -rf. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Delete with respect

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Delete
Commands & meaning
  • rmdir — removes only empty directories.
  • rm — removes files.
  • rm -r — recursively removes directories and contents.
  • rm -i — prompts before each deletion; use rm -ri for directories.
  • rm -rf — forceful, non-interactive recursive removal; use with extreme caution.
Warning
Never run rm -rf with an unverified path. Always confirm your working directory with pwd and check contents with ls before destructive commands.
Practice example
# Remove an empty directory
rmdir empty_dir
# Interactive remove of a directory tree
rm -ri conf
# Force remove a temporary backup (be sure this path is correct)
rm -rf /tmp/backup_logs
Key Takeaway
Use interactive flags while learning and keep backups. Alias dangerous commands only if you fully understand the consequences.

screens.title: File permissions and ownership — first look
screens.narratorSegment: Permissions and ownership determine who can read, write, or execute files and directories. Each file has an owner and a group; permissions are typically described for owner, group, and others. While we'll cover detailed permission modes later, now understand that incorrect ownership or permissions frequently cause application failures — for example, a web server that lacks write permission to its upload directory cannot save user uploads. The chown command changes ownership and chgrp changes group ownership, while chmod changes the permission bits. A concrete starter exercise: create a file, run ls -l to see its owner and mode, then use chown to change the owner and chmod to remove write permission for others. Misconception: changing permissions does not change who is billed for disk usage; it only changes access. Takeaway: validate permissions with ls -l after creating or moving files, and use chown and chmod to ensure applications have the access they need. File permissions and ownership — first look means permissions and ownership control access. use ls -l to inspect, chown to change ownership, and chmod to set who can read, write, or execute.. In practical terms, why chmod and chown matter when files are used by services and users. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Permissions matter
keyIdea.text: Permissions and ownership control access. Use ls -l to inspect, chown to change ownership, and chmod to set who can read, write, or execute.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Permissions
Core concept

Every file and directory has owner and group metadata and permission bits that govern read, write, and execute access for owner, group, and others.

Quick check
ls -l README.md
# -rw-r--r-- 1 alice dev  234 Aug 10 10:00 README.md
chown webuser:webgroup /var/www/my_app
chmod 750 /var/www/my_app
Why it matters
Incorrect permissions often lead to services failing to read or write required files. Fixing ownership and mode is a common system administration task.
Practice scenario
Create a file as your user, view ls -l to confirm owner and mode, then use chown to assign it to the service account and chmod to restrict write access, confirming the service can still function.
Key Takeaway
Always verify ownership and permissions after moving or copying files, because permissions may need adjustment for services to work correctly.

screens.title: Guided hands-on walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: This guided exercise walks through a complete sequence you can run in a disposable environment. Start by moving to your home directory, create a my_project folder, then build nested directories with mkdir -p. Create placeholder files with touch and verify the tree with ls -R. Next, copy config. properties to config. bak using cp and copy the logs directory into /tmp as a safe backup with cp -r. Use mv to rename README. md to PROJECT_INFO. md and to move source directories as needed. For deletion practice, use rm -ri on conf to experience interactive prompts and then remove the temporary backup in /tmp with rm -rf only after confirming its path. Throughout, check ownership and modes with ls -l, and experiment with chown and chmod to see how access changes. The core learning is sequencing: create, verify, copy, move, and delete, always verifying at each step. Misconception: treating rm -rf as safe because you used it once; always verify location before running it. End with a reflective check: can you repeat the sequence in a disposable directory without losing important files?

keyIdea.title: Practice sequence
keyIdea.text: Create a project scaffold, copy backups, move and rename, then practice safe deletion with interactive prompts and final confirmation for forceful removal.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Lab Walkthrough
Terminal steps
cd ~
mkdir my_project
cd my_project
mkdir -p src/main/java conf logs
touch src/main/java/App.java conf/config.properties logs/app.log README.md
ls -R
cp conf/config.properties conf/config.bak
cp -r logs /tmp/backup_logs/
mv README.md PROJECT_INFO.md
rm -ri conf
# after prompts
rm -rf /tmp/backup_logs

Commands to verify

screens.title: Backups and conservative habits

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we focus on the practical command-line actions you'll use every day as a system administrator. You will learn how to create files and nested directories quickly, copy and move items with predictable behavior, and delete safely while avoiding catastrophic mistakes. We also introduce basic file permissions and ownership so you can control who can access what. For each command you'll see a concise example you can reproduce in a terminal, plus a common mistake to watch for. Practically speaking, these operations enable installing software, configuring services, organising projects, and carrying out cleanups without breaking other users or services. A concrete example: creating a project layout with mkdir -p, adding starter files with touch, backing up configuration with cp -r, and then moving or renaming files with mv. We emphasize safety: use rm -ri when unsure and keep reliable backups. By the end of this chapter you'll perform these tasks confidently, understand the permissions implications, and avoid the most dangerous pitfalls.

By the end of this chapter you will reliably create and remove files and directories from the command line, copy and move data with intent, and understand when deletion is dangerous. Objective one makes you comfortable creating files and nested directories using touch and mkdir -p; this matters because consistent structure reduces mistakes when configuring services. Objective two focuses on copying and moving with cp and mv, including recursive copying; knowing the difference prevents accidental duplication or data loss. Objective three teaches safe deletion patterns and interactive flags such as rm -ri; this prevents accidental catastrophic removals and builds a habit of double-checking paths. Objective four introduces the basics of permissions and ownership so you can ensure the right users and services have appropriate access. Each objective pairs a command with a short scenario you can practice in a terminal, and a verification step such as ls -R to confirm changes. These skills are essential daily tasks for a system administrator and form the foundation for later topics like automation and backups.

This second objectives slide frames the same four learning outcomes as hands-on tasks so you leave this chapter with muscle memory. First, create a nested directory and files, then verify with ls -R; this shows how mkdir -p and touch become a reproducible project pattern. Second, copy and move data: practice cp -r to duplicate a logs directory, then use mv to relocate and rename a file — notice mv changes the original location rather than creating a second copy. Third, deletion safety: run rm -ri on a disposable directory to experience interactive prompts and contrast that with rm -rf to see why force removes prompts. Always confirm your current directory before destructive commands. Fourth, permissions and ownership: create a file, observe owner and mode with ls -l, then use chown and chmod to adjust and retest access. Each task includes a verification step and a simple mnemonic, reinforcing safe habits that prevent most common admin errors.

Creating files and directories is one of the most frequent tasks you'll perform. The touch command creates an empty file when it doesn't exist and updates timestamps when it does; this is useful for quickly making placeholder files like README. md or logs/app. log. For directories, mkdir creates a single directory; adding the -p option lets you create a full nested path in one command. For example, mkdir -p projects/my_app/config builds every required parent automatically. This is faster and less error-prone than running multiple mkdir commands. A common misconception is that touch is only for empty files; in reality it also updates access and modification times which can be useful in build systems. A concrete example: mkdir -p src/main/java conf logs followed by touch src/main/java/App. java conf/config. properties logs/app. log creates a reproducible starter layout. Verification with ls -R shows the created tree. Tip: when scripting, mkdir -p prevents errors if the directory already exists. Takeaway: use touch for files and mkdir -p for nested directories to set up consistent structures quickly and predictably. Creating files and directories means use touch to create or update files and mkdir -p to create nested directories in a single, idempotent command.. In practical terms, using touch and mkdir -p to build and initialize project structures. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Copying is often used for backups, testing, or preparing alternate configurations. The cp command copies files with a simple source and destination syntax. For directories you must add -r to copy recursively, for example cp -r my_app_dir /srv/backup/ will duplicate the directory and its contents into the backup location. A common error is forgetting the -r option and receiving an error that the source is a directory. Another pitfall is confusing cp with mv: cp leaves the original intact while mv relocates it. A concrete example from the hands-on activity: cp conf/config. properties conf/config. bak creates a backup copy in place, while cp -r logs /tmp/backup_logs copies the whole logs tree. Verify copies via ls or by checking file sizes and counts. If you need to preserve permissions and timestamps, additional options exist, but at this stage remember the core difference: cp duplicates, mv moves. Misconception check: cp does not change ownership of the original file; it creates a new file owned by the user who ran the command unless special options are used. Takeaway: use cp -r for directories and always verify the destination.

Moving and renaming are both handled by the mv command. The simplest form is mv source destination. If the destination is a new name in the same directory, mv performs a rename. If the destination is a directory path, mv relocates the source into that directory. Unlike cp, mv does not create a separate copy; it changes the filesystem location or name reference of the original. This behavior makes mv efficient for reorganizing files but also means that a mistaken mv can make the original path disappear. For example, mv old_name. txt new_name. txt renames a file, and mv config. yaml /etc/my_app/ moves it to the configuration directory. A common misconception is thinking mv requires -r for directories; it does not — moving a directory will move all contents implicitly. In scripts, adding checks such as testing destination existence or using mv -n to prevent overwriting can protect data. Always verify results with ls -R or by opening the moved files in their new location. Takeaway: mv moves or renames without duplication; use it when you want to reorganize rather than copy.

Deletion is the most dangerous daily operation if used without caution. Use rmdir only for empty directories; it fails if the directory contains files. For files, rm removes single files. To remove directories and their contents, rm -r recursively deletes everything inside. The -i flag makes rm interactive and prompts before each deletion, which can be a lifesaver when working in unfamiliar directories. The rm -rf combination is both recursive and forceful and will delete without prompts even for write-protected files — this is why rm -rf used in the wrong path can be catastrophic. A concrete example from the hands-on activity: rm -ri conf prompts you for each file before deleting, providing a safety net. Contrast that with rm -rf /tmp/backup_logs which deletes without confirmation. Misconception: some users expect the shell to prevent dangerous rm commands; it will not. Always double-check pwd and consider an alias or a habit of running ls before rm. Takeaway: prefer interactive removal during learning and retain backups to recover from mistakes. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Permissions and ownership determine who can read, write, or execute files and directories. Each file has an owner and a group; permissions are typically described for owner, group, and others. While we'll cover detailed permission modes later, now understand that incorrect ownership or permissions frequently cause application failures — for example, a web server that lacks write permission to its upload directory cannot save user uploads. The chown command changes ownership and chgrp changes group ownership, while chmod changes the permission bits. A concrete starter exercise: create a file, run ls -l to see its owner and mode, then use chown to change the owner and chmod to remove write permission for others. Misconception: changing permissions does not change who is billed for disk usage; it only changes access. Takeaway: validate permissions with ls -l after creating or moving files, and use chown and chmod to ensure applications have the access they need. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
